paragraphs: Swamiji said there are two kinds of courage. One is the courage to stand in front of a cannon. The other, rarer kind comes from deep spiritual conviction.

He told of an emperor who invaded India. His teacher had asked him to meet some of the country's sages while he was there. After searching for a long time, the emperor found one: a very old man seated on a block of stone. They talked for a while, and the emperor was so struck by the old man's wisdom that he invited him to come back to his own country.

The sage declined. He was perfectly content in his forest. The emperor offered money, rank and riches, reminding him that he was the ruler of the world. The sage said no again; such things did not interest him. Finally the emperor threatened him: come with me, or I will kill you.

The old man smiled calmly. That, he said, was the most foolish thing the emperor had said yet. No one could kill him. The sun could not dry him up, fire could not burn him, and a sword could not cut him, for he was the Spirit that is never born, never dies, and is present everywhere. Swamiji called this spiritual boldness, as opposed to the courage of a lion or tiger.

He gave one more example. During the uprising of 1857, a great Swami was badly stabbed by a Muslim mutineer. Some Hindu mutineers caught the attacker, dragged him before the Swami and offered to kill him. The Swami only looked up at the man and said, "My brother, thou art He, thou art He!" Then he died.
learn: Physical bravery is admirable, but the deeper courage is to know who you are so clearly that threats, bribes and even violence cannot shake you. That inner security also makes forgiveness possible, even toward those who hurt you.
